chapters.title: Where would you look for peace?

items.say: If someone asked you where peace comes from, what would you say?
A quiet house? Money in the bank? Good news from the doctor? An end to the arguments in the family, or in the world?

Those are good things, and we pray for them. But they come and go. This second Sunday of Advent, many churches light the candle of peace. And so today we're going back to a promise about peace that was spoken into one of the darkest moments in Israel's history. You've probably heard its words read at Christmas: "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given:"
But do you know where those words were first spoken, and to whom? The story behind them makes them even more beautiful.
Isaiah lived about seven hundred years before Jesus was born. In his day, the great empire of the region was Assyria, and its armies were moving south.

The first places to fall were in the far north of Israel, the region around the Sea of Galilee, the lands of the tribes of Zebulun and Naphtali. The book of Second Kings records it. The Assyrian king came and took Galilee, all the land of Naphtali, "and carried them captive to Assyria."
Families were taken away. Towns were emptied. People who had lived by that lake for generations were marched off to a foreign land.
In Isaiah's words, it was a land of gloom and anguish. The end of chapter 8 describes people looking up to the sky and down at the earth, and seeing only trouble and darkness.
If you've ever been through a season where everything seemed to be taken from you, one thing after another, you can understand how they felt.

chapters.title: The people that walked in darkness

items.say: And then, right into that darkness, Isaiah speaks a promise that turns everything around.
"Nevertheless the dimness shall not be such as was in her vexation,"
Nevertheless. One of the great hope words of the Bible. The darkness was real. Nevertheless.
And the prophet goes on, naming the very same places that were hit first and hardest: Zebulun, Naphtali, "Galilee of the nations." And then:
"The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined."
Do you see what God is doing? The place that fell first is the place where the light will shine first. The region that suffered most is the one He singles out for hope.
Now fast forward seven hundred years.

A young man from Nazareth begins to teach. And where does He make His home? Matthew tells us. "And leaving Nazareth, he came and dwelt in Capernaum, which is upon the sea coast, in the borders of Zabulon and Nephthalim:"
The very same lands. Matthew quotes Isaiah directly: "The people which sat in darkness saw great light;"

Jesus started His public ministry in the place that had been in the shadow the longest. He walked those shores, called fishermen there, healed and taught there. The light Isaiah promised came, and it came to the forgotten corner first.
That's the first thing this passage tells us about peace. God's peace doesn't wait for us to get out of the dark. The light comes into it.

chapters.title: Unto us a child is born

items.say: And how does the light come? Isaiah's answer is surprising.
Not with an army. Isaiah says the noise of battle and the garments rolled in blood will be burned as fuel for the fire, gone for good.
Instead: "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder:"
A child. The answer to the empire's power is a baby. The answer to the battle is a birth.

It sounds weak. But it's the way God chose. And when the angels finally announced His birth to shepherds near Bethlehem, what was their song? "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men."
Peace arrived in a manger.
Then Isaiah gives this child four names, and each one tells us something about the peace He brings.
"and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace."
Wonderful, Counsellor. When you don't know what to do, He is the One with wisdom. You don't need to have every answer to have peace. You need to know the One who does.
The mighty God. Peace isn't the same as weakness. The child in the manger is mighty, strong enough to carry the government on His shoulder, and strong enough to carry you.
The everlasting Father. Not a ruler who comes and goes like the kings of Isaiah's day. He doesn't change, and He doesn't leave.
The Prince of Peace. The last name gathers up all the others. His whole reign is peace.
The next verse adds something that's easy to miss.
"Of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end,"
No end. Earthly peace treaties are signed and broken. Quiet seasons in our lives come and go. But the peace of His kingdom keeps growing, and never runs out.
And Isaiah ends with a promise of who will make it happen. Not us. "The zeal of the LORD of hosts will perform this."
That takes a weight off our shoulders. We're invited to be peacemakers, but we're not the ones holding the world's peace together. He is.

chapters.title: Peace in your own dark places

items.say: So what does this mean for you, this Advent?

Maybe your own life has a Galilee, a place that was hit first and hardest. A loss, a diagnosis, a broken relationship, a long season of anxiety. Isaiah's message is that God's light shines first in exactly those places.

It's worth saying gently: the peace Jesus gives isn't a promise that every trouble will disappear before Christmas. On the night before He died, He told His friends, "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid."
Not as the world giveth. The world's peace depends on everything going well. His peace can live in us even when things are hard.
And if your heart is very troubled right now, please reach out to someone you trust, a pastor, a friend, a counselor, or a local helpline. God often brings His peace through people He puts beside us.
Here's something to try this week. When worry rises, pray the four names, one with each breath. Wonderful Counsellor. Mighty God. Everlasting Father. Prince of Peace.
Let's pray.

Lord Jesus, Prince of Peace, You came as a child into a dark world, and You came first to the places that had suffered most. Shine Your light into the dark places of our lives today. Be our Wonderful Counsellor when we don't know the way. Be our Mighty God when we are weak. Be our Everlasting Father when everything else is changing. And give us Your peace, not as the world gives, but as only You can. Make us peacemakers in our homes and in our neighbourhoods this Christmas season. And let Your peace keep growing in us, with no end. In Your name we pray, Amen.
If there's a dark place you'd like us to pray for, share it in the comments, even in a word. And keep walking with us every day on the road to Christmas. God bless you.
